extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Euclidean geometry / readers of classical mathematical treatises
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and organizing geometric demonstrations in the Euclidean style: which propositions to derive from which predecessors, how to construct auxiliary lines/circles, and what kinds of argumentation and rhetorical devices are appropriate or inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and firmness of demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations must have utility and a firm, invincible foundation; works that rest on oracles, poetry, magic, or ambiguous authorities are to be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts serious natural-rational demonstrations with authors who 'petere... ab oraculis & poetarum' or rely on 'magia' and numerology (e.g., Agrippa). It states: 'Eaenim quz scribuntur seria habere debenr; utilitatem certum sine myinexpugnabile fundamentum.' Anti-pattern: basing arguments on ambiguous authorities, mystical numerology or poetic sound rather than demonstrable reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'inutilibus subtilitatibus' (useless subtleties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not indulge in subtleties that are merely curious or ostentatious without practical use or demonstrable foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise's theme 'De inutilibus subtillitatibus' criticizes arguments and inventions that are 'omnenn velletradere doctriná;nullá noffe' and praises moderation: subtlety may be tolerated when it adds useful variety or insight but should not replace demonstrable content. Example anti-patterns: creating constructions solely to astonish or to entangle respondents in sophistical questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build proofs from previously demonstrated propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each new proposition should be derived from earlier, demonstrated propositions; proofs must show dependencies explicitly (use Euclid's ordering where relevant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple passages describe how certain Euclidean propositions 'require' previous ones (e.g., 'Cüm igitur dormit homo...'; later: 'quod ad demonstrationem attinet, sola quarta... indiget' and long sequences of which Euclid propositions feed into which). Guidance: plan demonstrations so antecedent propositions supply necessary lemmas; indicate which prior items are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide complex demonstrations into manageable parts/lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Split difficult or long propositions into intermediate lemmas or parts and demonstrate each in turn before assembling the whole proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly instructs dividing ('diuidemus eam bifaria', 'diuidemus eam bifariá') and shows how large targets are achieved by a chain of propositions (e.g., numbering sequences of Euclid's propositions and reducing the new result to several previously-demonstrated steps). Practical note: explicitly state and prove intermediate claims so no hidden gaps remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geometric constructions (lines, circles, perpendiculars, diameters) as auxiliary devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce auxiliary constructions—drawing circles, erecting perpendiculars, producing diameters or centers—when they enable the required demonstration or construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author prescribes concrete constructions: finding centers, erecting perpendiculars to a given line, producing diameters, inscribing/circumscribing circles, and using these constructions to reduce problems (e.g., 'demonstrare... perpendicularem erigere... ad peripheriam circuli perueniet'). Practical guidance: incorporate explicit construction steps and justify them by prior propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit similarity and proportionality (similar triangles, mean proportionals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proportional relations and similar triangles as core tools for relating lengths and inferring equalities needed in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise uses proportional language frequently ('c M esse proportionalem inter c & c8', 'media proportio'), constructs mean proportionals, and obtains equalities of segments/ratios to effect geometric conclusions. Guidance: reduce metric claims to proportional relations between segments and use known similarity/proportion theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reductio/ad absurdum where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When denying the proposition leads to an impossibility, conclude the affirmative by contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text indicates using contradiction to rule out alternatives ('qui contradicenté deducat ad impossibile'); practical method: assume the contrary, derive an impossibility using prior propositions or proportional relations, then conclude the original claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures and inscriptions to aid comprehension and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide diagrams (figures) with clear labels and, where helpful, inscriptions or mnemonic devices; figures both contain the 'sense' and help memory of constructions and arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier sections discuss memory and figures: 'Figuræ contenta:fic cruces;arbores...' and 'memoria quafi intellectui similior eft.' Guidance: include clear, well-labelled figures and, where beneficial, verbal tags or numbered steps so readers can follow and recall the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about which case or configuration is treated
rubrics_metrics.description: State the exact configuration (which lines/circles/angles are given, which are constructed) and whether one is treating a general case or a special subcase; avoid implicit assumptions about placement or sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise repeatedly specifies loci (e.g., 'ex puncto datum', 'circuli... in circunferentia illius') and partitioning choices; guidance: specify centers, endpoints, which circle is inscribed/circumscribed, and whether elements lie inside or outside circles to prevent ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer proofs that produce general constructions rather than single numerical examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, present constructions and demonstrations that apply generically (construct a center, erect a perpendicular) rather than relying on special numerical coincidences or non-general cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author stresses producing constructions that 'non est opus nisi in circumscribendis aut inscribendis circulis, nisi centri inuentione' and objects to arguments that only show existence in special incidental instances. Guidance: aim for constructions and proofs that generalize across the intended domain (all circles, all triangles of a type).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order demonstrations to minimize repetition and exploit symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange steps and choose constructions so that symmetric or repetitive parts are handled uniformly and earlier lemmas serve multiple later propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise structures long chains of propositions so previous results are reused ('inde per vigesimam... demóstrabimus'), and advises decomposing results in ways that allow repeating a construction in many places rather than reproving similar facts. Practical tip: factor out common subproofs into lemmas used across the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure completeness: demonstrate all propositions needed to avoid hidden appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not leave intermediate claims unproven; if a step appeals to a fact 'already demonstrated', either cite the exact prior proposition or supply the short proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes verifying which of Euclid's propositions are needed and demonstrating those that are not already established ('quædem non aliis nisi demonstratis iam hucusque indigent'). Anti-pattern: assuming results without citation or skipping lemmas because they 'seem obvious'.
